questions.problem:
The probability mass function of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given below.
$x$ $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$ $4$
$f(x)$ $0.1$ $0.2$ $0.25$ $0.15$ $0.3$

$y$ $2$ $4$ $6$
$f(y)$ $0.25$ $0.5$ $0.25$

Find $\text{E}[5X+4Y].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables (not necessarily independent), and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y].
$$

First, let's find $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{E}[Y].$ If $X$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{x},$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{x}}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =0\cdot 0.1+1\cdot 0.2+2\cdot 0.25+3\cdot 0.15+4\cdot 0.3 \\  & =2.35.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{y},$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot f(y) \\  & =2\cdot 0.25+4\cdot 0.5+6\cdot 0.25 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X+4Y] & =\text{E}[5X]+\text{E}[4Y] \\  & =5\text{E}[X]+4\text{E}[Y] \\  & =5\cdot 2.35+4\cdot 4 \\  & =27.75.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{x}}x\cdot f(x) \\  & =1\cdot \frac{1}{6}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}+3\cdot \frac{1}{6}+4\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, if $Y$ is defined on a sample space ${S}_{y},$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{y}}y\cdot f(y) \\  & =1\cdot \frac{5}{8}+5\cdot \frac{1}{8}+10\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
In a factory, two machines independently produce the same product. The random variable $X$ represents the number of rejects per day of the first machine, and the random variable $Y$ is the number of rejects per day on another machine. The probability distributions of $X$ and $Y$ are given below.
$x$ $0$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$f(x)$ $0.1$ $0.6$ $0.2$ $0.1$
$y$ $0$ $1$ $2$
$f(y)$ $0.5$ $0.3$ $0.2$

Calculate the expected number of items per day that the factory rejects.
questions.worked_solution:
We need to calculate $\text{E}[X+Y].$

Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables (not necessarily independent), and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y].
$$

The expected values of $X$ and $Y$ are calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot 0.1+1\cdot 0.6+2\cdot 0.2+3\cdot 0.1=1.3 \\ \text{E}[Y] & =0\cdot 0.5+1\cdot 0.3+2\cdot 0.2=0.7\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get

$$
\text{E}[X+Y]=\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y]=1.3+0.7=2.
$$

questions.problem: Michael has two card decks. One of them contains five cards, the cards are labeled with numbers $0,$ $2,$ $4,$ $6,$ and $8$, and the other deck contains four cards, labeled with numbers $1,$ $3,$ $5,$ and $7.$ From each of the two decks one card is randomly drawn. What is the expected value of the sum of the numbers of the cards?
questions.worked_solution:
We need to calculate $\text{E}[X+Y].$

Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are random variables (not necessarily independent), and $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\text{E}[aX+bY]=a\text{E}[X]+b\text{E}[Y].
$$

Let the random variable $X$ be the number of the card drawn from the first deck, and the random variable $Y$ be the number of the card drawn from the second deck.

The expected values of $X$ and $Y$ are calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot \frac{1}{5}+2\cdot \frac{1}{5}+4\cdot \frac{1}{5}+6\cdot \frac{1}{5}+8\cdot \frac{1}{5}=4 \\ \text{E}[Y] & =1\cdot \frac{1}{4}+3\cdot \frac{1}{4}+5\cdot \frac{1}{4}+7\cdot \frac{1}{4}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get

$$
\text{E}[X+Y]=\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y]=4+4=8.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot 0.4+2\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.2=1.8 \\ \text{E}[Y] & =0\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.3+4\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.1=1.8\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Marcus has two spinners. The first of them has three sections labeled $1,2,3,$ and the second has four sections labeled $0,2,4,8.$ The random variable $X$ represents the number obtained on a typical throw of the first spinner, and $Y$ is the number obtained on a typical throw of the second spinner. The first spinner is rolled $10$ times, and the second spinner is rolled $5$ times. What is the expected value of the sum of all outcomes?
$x$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$f(x)$ $0.4$ $0.4$ $0.2$
$y$ $0$ $2$ $4$ $8$
$f(y)$ $0.5$ $0.3$ $0.1$ $0.1$
questions.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ be the $i$th score obtained from the first spinner, and let ${Y}_{j}$ be the $j$th score obtained from the second spinner. Then, we need to calculate 

$$
\text{E}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{X}_{i}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{5}{Y}_{j}].
$$

Using the properties of expected value, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{10}{X}_{i}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{5}{Y}_{j}] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{10}\text{E}[{X}_{i}]+{\sum }_{j=1}^{5}\text{E}[{Y}_{j}] \\  & =10\text{E}[X]+5\text{E}[Y],\end{aligned}
$$

where the last equality above is true because $\text{E}[{X}_{i}]=\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{E}[{Y}_{j}]=\text{E}[Y]$ for all $1\le i\le 10,\,1\le j\le 5.$

The expected values of $X$ and $Y$ are calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot 0.4+2\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.2=1.8 \\ \text{E}[Y] & =0\cdot 0.5+2\cdot 0.3+4\cdot 0.1+8\cdot 0.1=1.8\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get

$$
\text{E}[10X+5Y]=10\text{E}[X]+5\text{E}[Y]=10\cdot 1.8+5\cdot 1.8=27.
$$

questions.problem: For the independent random variables $X$ and $Y,$ we have $\text{E}[X]=-3$ and $\text{E}[Y]=2.$ Find $\text{E}[XY].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are *independent* random variables, then

$$
\text{E}[X\cdot Y]=\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y]
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, we have

$$
\text{E}[X\cdot Y]=\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y]=-3\cdot 2=-6.
$$

questions.problem:
The probability distributions of the independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given below.
$x$ $5$ $6$ $9$
$f(x)$ $\frac{1}{5}$ $\frac{2}{5}$ $\frac{2}{5}$
$y$ $0$ $3$ $6$
$f(y)$ $\frac{1}{8}$ $\frac{1}{4}$ $\frac{5}{8}$

Find $\text{E}[XY].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are *independent* random variables, then

$$
\text{E}[X\cdot Y]=\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y]
$$

The expected values of $X$ and $Y$ are calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5}+6\cdot \frac{2}{5}+9\cdot \frac{2}{5}=7 \\ \text{E}[Y] & =0\cdot \frac{1}{8}+3\cdot \frac{1}{4}+6\cdot \frac{5}{8}=\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, we have

$$
\text{E}[X\cdot Y]=\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y]=7\cdot \frac{9}{2}=\frac{63}{2}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Compute $\textrm E[5X-2Y]$ if $\textrm E[X]=1$ and $\textrm E[Y] = 2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For any random variables $X,Y$ and any constants $a,b,$ we have

$$
\textrm E[aX+bY] = a \textrm E[X] + b \textrm E[Y].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[5X-2Y] & =5\text{E}[X]-2\text{E}[Y] \\  & =5(1)-2(2) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Expected Value of a Sum of Random Variables in Context
canonical_examples.problem:
Andrea has two dice. One of them is fair, and the other is not. The rolls of the unfair die follow the probability mass function $f(y)$ shown in the table below. What is the expected sum of the outcomes of $2$ throws of the fair die and $4$ throws of the unfair one?

| $y$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(y)$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ | $\dfrac{1}{16}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ | $\dfrac{1}{8}$ | $\dfrac{1}{4}$ | $\dfrac{1}{16}$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $X_i$ be the $i$th score obtained from the fair die, and let $Y_j$ be the $j$th score obtained from the unfair die. Also, let $X$ and $Y$ represent the scores obtained from a typical throw of the fair and unfair die, respectively.

Then, we need to calculate 

$$
\textrm E\left[
\sum_{i=1}^2 X_i + \sum_{j=1}^4 Y_j
\right].
$$

Using the properties of expected value, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{X}_{i}+{\sum }_{j=1}^{4}{Y}_{j}] & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{2}\text{E}[{X}_{i}]+{\sum }_{j=1}^{4}\text{E}[{Y}_{j}] \\  & =2\text{E}[X]+4\text{E}[Y],\end{aligned}
$$

where the last equality above is true because $\textrm E[X_i] = \textrm E[X]$ and $\textrm E[Y_j] = \textrm E[Y]$ for all $1\leq i \leq 2,\: 1\leq j\leq 4.$

The expected values of $X$ and $Y$ are calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot \frac{1}{6}+2\cdot \frac{1}{6}+3\cdot \frac{1}{6}+4\cdot \frac{1}{6}+5\cdot \frac{1}{6}+6\cdot \frac{1}{6}=\frac{7}{2} \\ \text{E}[Y] & =1\cdot \frac{1}{4}+2\cdot \frac{1}{16}+3\cdot \frac{1}{4}+4\cdot \frac{1}{8}+5\cdot \frac{1}{4}+6\cdot \frac{1}{16}=\frac{13}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get

$$
\textrm E[2X+4Y]=2\textrm E[X]+4\textrm E[Y]= 2\cdot \dfrac{7}{2}+4\cdot \dfrac{13}{4} =20.
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Expected Value of a Product of Random Variables
canonical_examples.problem:
The probability distributions of the independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ are given below.
$x$ $-4$ $-2$ $2$ $4$
$f(x)$ $\dfrac{1}{6}$ $\dfrac{1}{3}$ $\dfrac{1}{3}$ $\dfrac{1}{6}$
$y$ $1$ $2$ $3$
$f(y)$ $\dfrac{1}{4}$ $\dfrac{1}{4}$ $\dfrac{1}{2}$

Find $\textrm E[XY].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if $X$ and $Y$ are *independent* random variables, then

$$
\textrm E[X\cdot Y]=\textrm E[X]\cdot \textrm E[Y].
$$

The expected values of $X$ and $Y$ are calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =-4\cdot \frac{1}{6}-2\cdot \frac{1}{3}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{6}=0 \\ \text{E}[Y] & =1\cdot \frac{1}{4}+2\cdot \frac{1}{4}+3\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $X$ and $Y$ are independent, we have

$$
\textrm E[X\cdot Y] = \textrm E[X] \cdot \textrm E[Y] = 0  \cdot \dfrac{9}{4} = 0.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We can use the following property to simplify expressions involving expected values:

For any random variables $X$ and $Y$ and constants $a$ and $b,$ we have

$$
\textrm E[aX+bY] = a \textrm E[X] + b \textrm E[Y].
$$

In other words, the expected value of a sum of scaled random variables equals the sum of the scaled expected values.

For example, 

$$
\textrm E[2X+5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] + 5 \textrm E[Y].
$$

Note that the property also works with subtraction:

$$
\textrm E[2X-5Y] = 2 \textrm E[X] - 5 \textrm E[Y]
$$

We can extend this idea to any number of random variables. For example, for any random variables $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,$ and real constants $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$, we have

$$
\textrm{E}[a_1X_1+a_2X_2+\cdots+ a_nX_n]= a_1\textrm E[X_1]+a_2\textrm E[X_2]+\cdots +a_n\textrm{E}[X_n],
$$

or more concisely,

$$
\textrm{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i X_i\right] =\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \textrm E[X_i].
$$

Note that the random variables  $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n,$ are *not* required to be independent.

tutorials.name: The Expectation of a Product of Random Variables
tutorials.problem:
The expected value of the product of two *independent* random variables is equal to the product of the expected values. So, if the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are independent, we have

$$
\textrm{E}[X\cdot Y] = \textrm E[X]\cdot \textrm E[Y].
$$

For example, if we know that $X$ are $Y$ are independent, and that $\textrm E[X]=2$ and $\textrm E[Y]=3$, then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\cdot Y] & =\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

When working with the expected value of a product of random variables, it's important to check that the variables are independent. The formula above is *not* true if $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.

More generally, if the random variables $X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n$ are *mutually* independent, then

$$
\textrm E[X_1\cdot X_2 \cdots  X_n]=\textrm E[X_1]\cdot \textrm E[X_2]\cdot\ldots\cdot \textrm E[X_n],
$$

or more concisely,

$$
\textrm{E}\left[ \prod_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \prod_{i=1}^n \textrm E[X_i],
$$

where $\prod$ is the product operator.
